samples.prompt: Write a short informal essay that uses humorous personal anecdotes to illustrate broader observations about human nature, social customs, or how people's circumstances influence their behavior.
samples.generated:
We were in the habit of talking with <PERSON> on Sunday mornings at his
place, when we were all together. One day he said to me: "You have been
very kind to me; you have given me something to eat. Now I am going to
give you something." He went out, returned in a short while, and brought
with him an enormous piece of raw hams, which he set down in the middle
of the table. Then he sat down opposite me, took up a knife, and
started to cut off slices for himself. I looked at him, saying:
"Sir, what will you do with this ham?"

"I'll give it to you," he replied.

"That's a good idea," I said; "I'll accept your offer."

"Why, I'm going to eat it myself," said the other.

"Well, if you don't intend to divide it," said I, "it is of no use to
you. I don't want it."

"I shall eat it anyway," said the other. "It belongs to me."

I didn't understand this. But he explained. "It was my father who gave
me this ham, and if I die without eating it I'll never be happy."

I said nothing; but I was greatly impressed by this remark and by the
custom to which it referred. It seems to me that all men have a right to
eat all they like, whether they die or live, and if they do not they
have no right to complain.

samples.prompt: Write a candid reflection on the gap between public perception and private reality, using humor and irony to explore personal vanity.
samples.generated:
I do not know whether I am to be admired or pitied. The world thinks I am
to be admired, but I think they are mistaken.

When I was young--that is, when I was about six years old--I used to get
a great deal of pleasure out of making faces at my mother. One time she
said, "Do you want to see my teeth?" I said, "No." She said, "Well, take
them out," and so I did; and then she said, "You are too young to do
it now."

I have always been vain about my teeth ever since that time. I don't
think I've ever been able to overcome that feeling. It is a natural
thing, I suppose, because I am proud of those teeth which make me look
so distinguished and important. But the reason I have been able to
overcome it is not because I am ashamed of them--I'm not ashamed of
them--but because I don't care anything about them. That is to say,
they haven't any good points about them to speak of, so I don't care
anything about them. They haven't any of the qualities which make a
set of teeth desirable. They are small, and not very white; they have
no character; they're not at all distinguished-looking, or handsome.
They're plain, common, ordinary teeth, like everyone else's teeth. So I
don't care anything about them.

Judge <PERSON> seems to have all the virtues that he ascribes to me. But,
oh my! if you could throw an X-ray through him. We are a pair. I have
made a life-study of trying to appear to be what he seems to think I am.
Everybody believes that I am a monument of all the virtues, but it is
nothing of the sort. I am living two lives, and it keeps me pretty busy.

Some day there will be a chairman who will forget some of these merits
of mine, and then he will make a speech.

I have more personal vanity than modesty, and twice as much veracity as
the two put together.

When that fearless and forgetful chairman is found there will be another
story told. At <ORG> recently I thought that I had found
him. He started in in the way that I knew I should be painted with all
sincerity, and was leading to things that would not be to my credit; but
when he said that he never read a book of mine I knew at once that he
was a liar, because he never could have had all the wit and intelligence
with which he was blessed unless he had read my works as a basis.

I like compliments. I like to go home and tell them all over again to
the members of my family. They don't believe them, but I like to tell
them in the home circle, all the same. I like to dream of them if I can.

I thank everybody for their compliments, but I don't think that I am
praised any more than I am entitled to be.
